passages.text: CDK8/19 inhibition prevents adaptive resistance to CDK4/6 inhibitors <italic>in vitro</italic> and <italic>in vivo</italic>
Summary

Cyclin-dependent kinase 4/6 (CDK4/6) inhibitors have become a standard of care for estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer and are being developed for other malignancies. <sentence_start/>However, resistance to these drugs readily develops, limiting their impact on patient survival. <sentence_start/>Mechanisms of resistance to CDK4/6 inhibition involve multiple changes in gene expression. <sentence_start/>We investigated the process of tumor cell adaptation to CDK4/6 inhibitors and the impact of selective inhibitors of CDK8/19 Mediator kinases-broad-spectrum regulators of transcriptional reprogramming-on such adaptations. <sentence_start/>Adaptive non-genetic resistance to CDK4/6 inhibitors develops rapidly, but the addition of CDK8/19 inhibitors prevents the development of this resistance in different tumor models, <italic>in vitro</italic> and <italic>in vivo</italic>. <sentence_start/>RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) analysis reveals that combining CDK4/6 and CDK8/19 inhibitors suppresses many of the adaptation-associated changes in gene expression, including those previously associated with CDK4/6 inhibitor resistance. <sentence_start/>The findings suggest that CDK8/19 inhibition may greatly extend the therapeutic benefit of CDK4/6 inhibitors.
Graphical abstract
Highlights
CDK4/6 inhibitor resistance rapidly emerges through non-genetic adaptation
Resistance involves reversible transcriptional state switching
CDK8/19 inhibition suppresses adaptation-associated transcriptional reprogramming
CDK8/19 inhibitors enhance and prolong CDK4/6 inhibitor efficacy <italic>in vivo</italic>

Non-genetic adaptation curtails CDK4/6 inhibitor therapy. <sentence_start/>Mack et al. show that adaptive resistance arises through transcriptional reprogramming and is suppressed by inhibition of the Mediator kinases CDK8/19, which enhances CDK4/6 inhibitor efficacy <italic>in vitro</italic> and <italic>in vivo</italic>.
Introduction

Estrogen receptor-positive breast cancers (ER<sup>+</sup> BrCa) make up 70% of all breast cancers in the US. <sentence_start/>The most recent major class of drugs approved for ER<sup>+</sup> BrCa patients target cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) 4 and 6, which mediate G1/S checkpoint transition. <sentence_start/>CDK4/6 inhibitors (CDK4/6i) arrest the cell cycle and induce senescence by inhibiting phosphorylation of the Rb protein by the CDK4/6-cyclin D complex.<citation rid="bib1" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.molcel.2020.08.020" pmid="32946743" pmcid="PMC7582788" count="1"><sup>1</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Three CDK4/6i-palbociclib, ribociclib, and abemaciclib-have been approved for the treatment of ER<sup>+</sup> BrCa. <sentence_start/>Clinical and laboratory studies have shown that long-term treatment with CDK4/6i,<citation rid="bib2" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fphar.2025.1549520" pmcid="PMC12104243" pmid="40421216" count="1"><sup>2</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib3" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41388-025-03378-0" pmid="40200094" count="1"><sup>3</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib4" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12943-025-02226-9" pmid="39955556" pmcid="PMC11829392" count="1"><sup>4</sup></citation> as well as with a recently developed CDK4-specific inhibitor, atirmociclib,<citation rid="bib5" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ccell.2025.02.006" pmid="40068598" count="1"><sup>5</sup></citation> leads to drug resistance and reduced drug efficacy. <sentence_start/>It is now understood that the resistance to targeted drugs may first emerge as a non-genetic adaptation of tumor cells before stable resistant mutants can be selected.<citation rid="bib6" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41568-020-00302-4" pmid="33033407" count="1"><sup>6</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib7" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nature22794" pmid="28607484" pmcid="PMC5542814" count="1"><sup>7</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib8" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ccell.2020.12.002" pmid="33417832" pmcid="PMC8670073" count="1"><sup>8</sup></citation> Early adaptation to CDK4/6 inhibition, evidenced by continued S-phase entry in treated ER<sup>+</sup> BrCa, can occur as early as 72 h.<citation rid="bib9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/0008-5472.CAN-15-0728" pmid="27020857" pmcid="PMC5426059" count="1"><sup>9</sup></citation>

Mechanisms of both stable genetic resistance and transient transcriptional adaptation to CDK4/6i are varied and include acquired CDK6 amplification or overexpression,<citation rid="bib10" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/onc.2016.379" pmid="27748766" pmcid="PMC5393973" count="1"><sup>10</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib11" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/1078-0432.CCR-24-0036" pmid="39437014" pmcid="PMC11721435" count="1"><sup>11</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib12" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ccell.2018.11.006" pmid="30537512" pmcid="PMC6294301" count="1"><sup>12</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.celrep.2019.02.023" pmid="30840889" pmcid="PMC6449498" count="1"><sup>13</sup></citation> hyperphosphorylation of Rb by CDK2-cyclin E,<citation rid="bib14" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41698-022-00311-6" pmid="36153348" pmcid="PMC9509389" count="1"><sup>14</sup></citation> gradual loss of Rb protein,<citation rid="bib15" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41523-018-0092-4" pmcid="PMC6261939" pmid="30511015" count="1"><sup>15</sup></citation> and amplification of PI3K/mTOR signaling<citation rid="bib16" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13058-020-01320-8" pmid="32795346" pmcid="PMC7427086" count="1"><sup>16</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib17" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.18632/oncotarget.28177" pmid="35035775" pmcid="PMC8754587" count="1"><sup>17</sup></citation> and E2F activity<citation rid="bib18" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.celrep.2023.113198" pmcid="PMC10757862" pmid="37865915" count="1"><sup>18</sup></citation>; such gradual transcriptional changes can be suppressed through pleiotropic transcriptional inhibition, in particular via inhibitors of CDK7<citation rid="bib19" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1172/JCI188839" pmcid="PMC12520673" pmid="40794455" count="1"><sup>19</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib20" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/1078-0432.CCR-23-2975" pmid="38381406" pmcid="PMC11061603" count="1"><sup>20</sup></citation> and CDK9.<citation rid="bib21" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/0008-5472.CAN-23-0650" pmid="37801608" pmcid="PMC10758688" count="1"><sup>21</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Palbociclib resistance has also been linked to the development of the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), whereby senescent cells secrete factors enabling the survival of their neighbors.<citation rid="bib22" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41580-024-00727-x" pmid="38654098" count="1"><sup>22</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Given the diversity of the mechanisms for CDK4/6i resistance, blocking any individual resistance mechanisms is unlikely to have a major impact on patient outcomes. <sentence_start/>Thus, a combinatorial treatment regimen that would prevent the multiple mechanisms of resistance to CDK4/6i simultaneously could greatly improve the current standard of care.

CDK8 or its paralog, CDK19, together with their binding partner, cyclin C (CCNC), and the proteins MED12 and MED13, form the regulatory CDK module of the transcriptional Mediator complex.<citation rid="bib23" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.tibs.2022.01.002" pmid="35193797" pmcid="PMC8939868" count="1"><sup>23</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>CDK8 and CDK19 Mediator kinases differ in their expression but have qualitatively similar functions, and both paralogs need to be inhibited to achieve a phenotypic effect.<citation rid="bib24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/nar/gkad538" pmid="37378433" pmcid="PMC10415139" count="1"><sup>24</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>In contrast to CDK4/6, CDK2, or CDK1, CDK8 and CDK19 regulate transcription but do not directly regulate cell cycle progression.<citation rid="bib23" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.tibs.2022.01.002" pmid="35193797" pmcid="PMC8939868" count="1"><sup>23</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Unlike other transcriptional CDKs, such as CDK7 or CDK9, Mediator kinases are not a part of the overall transcription machinery but regulate the Mediator complex levels and act as cofactors or modifiers of several transcription factors. <sentence_start/>In particular, CDK8 and CDK19 act as positive regulators of signal-induced transcription factors, such as NF-κB, STATs, HIF1A, and ER, by promoting C-terminal domain phosphorylation of RNA Pol II, enabling pause-release and the elongation of transcription selectively in the context of genes activated by these transcription factors.<citation rid="bib24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/nar/gkad538" pmid="37378433" pmcid="PMC10415139" count="1"><sup>24</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.1710467114" pmid="28855340" pmcid="PMC5617299" count="1"><sup>25</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.18632/oncotarget.14894" pmid="28147342" pmcid="PMC5355036" count="1"><sup>26</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib27" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nsmb.1752" pmid="20098423" pmcid="PMC2920286" count="1"><sup>27</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib28" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2013.04.048" pmid="23746844" pmcid="PMC3681429" count="1"><sup>28</sup></citation> Through this mechanism, CDK8 and CDK19 were also shown to mediate SASP.<citation rid="bib29" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.1206906109" pmid="22869755" pmcid="PMC3427077" count="1"><sup>29</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Importantly, CDK8/19 inhibition downregulates primarily the signal-induced, but not basal, transcription of signal-activated genes, leading to the identification of CDK8/19 as pleiotropic regulators of transcriptional reprogramming.<citation rid="bib24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/nar/gkad538" pmid="37378433" pmcid="PMC10415139" count="1"><sup>24</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.1710467114" pmid="28855340" pmcid="PMC5617299" count="1"><sup>25</sup></citation> CDK8 and CDK19 also act as negative regulators of transcription, through post-transcriptional regulation of the Mediator complex subunits.<citation rid="bib24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/nar/gkad538" pmid="37378433" pmcid="PMC10415139" count="1"><sup>24</sup></citation>

Consistent with the effect of Mediator kinases on transcriptional reprogramming, CDK8/19 inhibitors (CDK8/19i), a new class of agents undergoing clinical trials in solid tumors and leukemias ( : , , , and ), were found to prevent the development of resistance, and sometimes help overcome the already acquired resistance, to different classes of anticancer agents, including, among others, antiestrogens, androgen deprivation, ionizing radiation, and inhibitors of HER2, EGFR, MEK, ERK/MAPK, mTOR, and AKT.<citation rid="bib26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.18632/oncotarget.14894" pmid="28147342" pmcid="PMC5355036" count="1"><sup>26</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib30" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/cells10010144" pmid="33445730" pmcid="PMC7828184" count="1"><sup>30</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib31" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fcell.2020.00408" pmcid="PMC7304162" pmid="32596239" count="1"><sup>31</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib32" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/0008-5472.CAN-21-4309" pmid="36398965" pmcid="PMC9938728" count="1"><sup>32</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib33" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.2201073119" pmcid="PMC9371674" pmid="35914167" count="1"><sup>33</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib34" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.2414501121" pmcid="PMC11588072" pmid="39541354" count="1"><sup>34</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib35" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41698-024-00615-9" pmid="38822082" pmcid="PMC11143207" count="1"><sup>35</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1101/2023.08.08.552491" count="1"><sup>36</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>In light of these findings, we hypothesized that CDK8/19 inhibition could also prevent or help overcome the multiple non-genetic mechanisms implicated in tumor resistance to CDK4/6i. <sentence_start/>In the present study, we investigated the process of rapid non-genetic adaptation of tumor cells to CDK4/6i and the effect of CDK8/19i on such adaptations. <sentence_start/>Our results show that the non-genetic adaptation of tumor cells to palbociclib and other CDK4/6i is a robust, non-stochastic process driven by transcriptional reprogramming, which is fully prevented by the addition of CDK8/19i, both <italic>in vitro</italic> and <italic>in vivo</italic>. <sentence_start/>These results warrant the exploration of CDK8/19i administration as a general approach to preventing the development of resistance and extending the therapeutic efficacy of CDK4/6i.
Results
Tumor cells rapidly adapt to CDK4/6 inhibitors, and this adaptation is prevented by Mediator kinase inhibition

To investigate tumor cell adaptation to CDK4/6i, the ER<sup>+</sup> BrCa cell lines MCF-7 and ZR-75-1 and the colorectal cancer cell line SW-620 were chosen for their <italic>de novo</italic> sensitivity to CDK4/6i palbociclib.<citation rid="bib37" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ncomms15916" pmcid="PMC5490269" pmid="28653662" count="1"><sup>37</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>To inhibit CDK8/19 Mediator kinase, the majority of our studies used equipotent selective CDK8/19i analogs SNX631<citation rid="bib33" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.2201073119" pmcid="PMC9371674" pmid="35914167" count="1"><sup>33</sup></citation> and SNX631-6,<citation rid="bib36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1101/2023.08.08.552491" count="1"><sup>36</sup></citation> with the latter being a late-preclinical stage drug candidate. <sentence_start/>Traditionally, palbociclib-resistant cell lines are selected for 4-12 months, usually with gradually increasing palbociclib concentrations.<citation rid="bib10" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/onc.2016.379" pmid="27748766" pmcid="PMC5393973" count="1"><sup>10</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>However, we found that 20-day exposure to 125-500 nM palbociclib was sufficient to produce a loss of sensitivity in all three cell lines tested, as indicated by different assays. <sentence_start/>Strikingly, the addition of SNX631 at a concentration that produces only a weak growth inhibition by itself (500 nM) maintains growth arrest by all the tested palbociclib concentrations across all three cell lines (Figures 1A and 1B). <sentence_start/>The key results of these assays were confirmed by direct cell counting and crystal violet staining (Figures S1A-S2C). <sentence_start/>In 7-day assays, SNX631 produced only weak synergistic or additive effects with palbociclib (Figure S1D); its effects became highly significant only by day 19 (Figure 1A; Table S1), indicating the prevention of adaptive resistance rather than acute drug synergy.<sentence_start/>Figure 1

(C) 20-day SRB assays of MCF-7 cells treated with ribociclib (left) or abemaciclib (right).
(D) 21-day SRB assays of MCF-7 cells treated with the indicated CDK8/19 inhibitors ± palbociclib (PAL).
(E) Crystal violet-stained flasks of MCF-7 cells treated for 42 days with 500 nM palbociclib ±500 nM SNX631 or with SNX631 added later on day 7.

Data are represented as mean ± SEM.

Similar rapid adaptation and its prevention by SNX631 were observed with the other two FDA-approved CDK4/6i, ribociclib and abemaciclib (Figure 1C). <sentence_start/>The role of CDK8/19 inhibition in the prevention of palbociclib adaptation was confirmed using four other structurally distinct CDK8/19i, senexin B<citation rid="bib26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.18632/oncotarget.14894" pmid="28147342" pmcid="PMC5355036" count="1"><sup>26</sup></citation> (Figure S1E), senexin C,<citation rid="bib38" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1021/acs.jmedchem.1c01951" pmid="35114084" pmcid="PMC10042267" count="1"><sup>38</sup></citation> BI1347,<citation rid="bib39" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/1535-7163.MCT-19-0789" pmid="32024684" pmcid="PMC7661742" count="1"><sup>39</sup></citation> and compound 25<citation rid="bib40" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1021/acsmedchemlett.9b00480" pmid="32071678" pmcid="PMC7025388" count="1"><sup>40</sup></citation> (Figure 1D). <sentence_start/>These inhibitors, all of which act primarily on CDK8/19 but have different off-target effects, prevented palbociclib adaptation in MCF-7 cells, indicating that CDK819 was their common target responsible for the prevention of resistance.

Despite near-complete growth suppression by 500 nM palbociclib in MCF-7 cells after 7 days of treatment, drug-adapted colonies began to emerge by day 20, and the adapted cells reached confluence by day 42 (Figure 1E). <sentence_start/>Combination treatment with palbociclib and a CDK8/19i effectively prevented this adaptation. <sentence_start/>Notably, addition of SNX631 even 7 days after initiating palbociclib treatment markedly suppressed cell growth (Figure 1E), suggesting that Mediator kinase inhibition can either reverse early adaptive resistance or prevent its full establishment.

When MCF-7 cells adapted to 500 nM palbociclib for 42 days were replated into the same 20-day viability assay used for unselected cells, the resistance of these palbociclib-adapted (P-A) cells was not maintained (Figures 1F and 1G), indicating that the adaptive response was unstable and likely non-genetic, rather than a stable, mutation-driven resistance. <sentence_start/>The replated P-A cells underwent a similar adaptation process as unselected cells (Figure 1A), albeit at a slightly faster rate, and this adaptation was similarly prevented by co-treatment with 500 nM SNX631 (Figure 1G). <sentence_start/>The P-A cells retained the same sensitivity to CDK8/19i as the parental cells (Figure S1F).
Initial sensitivity and adaptation to palbociclib are subject to lineage plasticity, but clonal heterogeneity does not impact the effects of CDK8/19 inhibition

The known heterogeneity within the MCF-7 cell line in regard to chemotherapeutic response,<citation rid="bib41" ref-type="bibr" pmid="26026074" count="1"><sup>41</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib42" ref-type="bibr" pmid="33299647" doi="10.20892/j.issn.2095-3941.2020.0028" pmcid="PMC7721098" count="1"><sup>42</sup></citation> coupled with the transient nature of palbociclib adaptation seen in Figure 1G, led us to hypothesize that the adaptation to palbociclib may reflect a reversible non-genetic switch process. <sentence_start/>To study the effects of palbociclib and CDK8/19i in individual MCF-7 cells, the cells were plated at a low density (100 cells/cm<sup>2</sup>) and analyzed by real-time video microscopy for the formation of cell clusters over 14 days. <sentence_start/>Clusters of control cells showed relatively homogeneous proliferation rates (Figure S2A, left). <sentence_start/>No clusters formed under combination treatment. <sentence_start/>The cells plated in SNX631 alone formed many clusters, similarly to control. <sentence_start/>However, the CDK8/19i eventually halted cluster proliferation and reduced cluster size, suggesting cell death (Figure S2A, middle), unlike the moderate growth inhibition seen at high density (Figure 1A). <sentence_start/>In contrast, only 10 proliferating clusters emerged under 500 nM palbociclib, a ∼100-fold reduction in plating efficiency versus control. <sentence_start/>Eight of these clusters proliferated 2.75-fold slower than controls, one arrested, and one regained a control-like growth rate (Figure S2A, right). <sentence_start/>Because both compounds showed markedly greater effects at low density, we concluded that this assay did not faithfully model palbociclib adaptation observed under high-density conditions.

To investigate the nature of palbociclib adaptation using the Luria-Delbrück fluctuation test,<citation rid="bib7" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nature22794" pmid="28607484" pmcid="PMC5542814" count="1"><sup>7</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib43" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/genetics/28.6.491" pmid="17247100" pmcid="PMC1209226" count="1"><sup>43</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib44" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/2159-8290.CD-20-1265" pmid="34911733" pmcid="PMC8983469" count="1"><sup>44</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib45" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fmicb.2022.1050516" pmcid="PMC9942930" pmid="36824587" count="1"><sup>45</sup></citation> 44 clones of the parental MCF-7 population were generated via ultra-low-density plating (Figure S2B). <sentence_start/>All clones were expanded and subjected to a 7-day concentration-response viability assay at high cell density, with dose ranges of palbociclib defined by parental IC<sub>50</sub>, in the absence and in the presence of 500 nM SNX631 (Figure S3). <sentence_start/>The palbociclib IC<sub>50</sub> values varied widely among the clones (Figure 2A). <sentence_start/>For some highly resistant clones, cell viability did not fall below 50% at the highest tested concentration; so, the best-fit IC<sub>50</sub> values were estimated by non-linear regression. <sentence_start/>Clonal growth also varied in the absence of palbociclib but showed a little correlation with responses to palbociclib (Figure S2C), SNX631 (Figure S2D), or between the two drugs (Figure S2E). <sentence_start/>Importantly, 500 nM SNX631 potentiated the response to palbociclib in all clones, except a few that grew too slowly, for reliable analysis (Figure S3). <sentence_start/>Clone responses to 500 nM palbociclib alone and the combination were strongly correlated (r<sup>2</sup> = 0.82; Figure 2B), confirming that CDK8/19 inhibition augmented the antiproliferative effect of palbociclib. <sentence_start/>On the other hand, Bliss scores spanned positive, neutral, and negative values across the clones (Figure S2F), in agreement with the previous conclusion that the strong drug interaction becomes apparent only at the later time when palbociclib resistance emerges.<sentence_start/>Figure 2
Effects of CDK8/19 inhibition on palbociclib adaptation in MCF-7 clones

(A) Palbociclib IC<sub>50</sub> values (7-day sulforhodamine B [SRB] assays) for 44 clones (black) and the parental MCF-7 cell line (red). <sentence_start/>IC<sub>50</sub> values were calculated using non-linear regression (variable slope). <sentence_start/>Best-fit IC<sub>50</sub> values were estimated for clones that did not reach 50% inhibition within the dose range, but confidence intervals were undefined due to incomplete curve definition.

(B) Correlation between the effects of palbociclib and palbociclib + SNX631 across clones (7-day SRB assay). <sentence_start/>Correlation coefficients were determined by linear regression. <sentence_start/>The line of identity (x = y) is shown in blue.

(C) Dose-response curves and IC<sub>50</sub> values from initial experiments (R1) and subsequent replicates (R2 and R3), for parental MCF-7 cells and three clones that were initially insensitive to palbociclib.
(D) 20-day SRB analysis of initially palbociclib-insensitive clones, from R2 (top) and R3 (bottom) (see C).
Data are represented as mean ± SEM.

Variation between the clones’ response to palbociclib generally increased as the concentration was increased, plateauing at approximately 60% variation for all concentrations above 63 nM (Figure S4A). <sentence_start/>Treating clonal cells with 500 nM palbociclib revealed an inter-clonal variation that was moderately higher than the noise control (variations between biological repeats of the MCF-7 parental cell line treated with 500 nM palbociclib) but statistically significant (Figure S4B). <sentence_start/>If each cell’s adaptation response to CDK4/6i was purely random, we would have expected to see inter-clonal variations similar to the noise control. <sentence_start/>The non-skewed distributions of the palbociclib concentration response (Figure S4C) are consistent with the stochastic switching model of individual cells.

To confirm this conclusion, the three most palbociclib-resistant clones (18, 30, and 32) were retested twice after ∼17 generations of drug-free growth between assays. <sentence_start/>All three clones showed decreased IC<sub>50</sub> values in the second assay, followed by increased IC<sub>50</sub> values in the third (Figure 2C). <sentence_start/>In contrast, the parental MCF-7 population showed only minor IC<sub>50</sub> fluctuations, suggesting either that crosstalk between all subpopulations within MCF-7 prevents fluctuations in palbociclib sensitivity or that whatever fluctuations occur within the diverse cell lines result in regression to the mean IC<sub>50</sub>.

We also performed 20-day palbociclib adaptation assays for clones 18, 30, and 32, alongside the last two IC<sub>50</sub> measurements. <sentence_start/>All three clones continued proliferating in palbociclib, consistent with adaptation, but remained arrested by the addition of SNX631 (Figure 2D). <sentence_start/>Their response to the combination was even stronger than that of the parental line, indicating that Mediator kinase inhibition consistently prevents palbociclib adaptation despite variation in palbociclib sensitivity among MCF-7 subpopulations.
<italic>In vivo</italic> treatment with Mediator kinase inhibitor strongly potentiates palbociclib in palbociclib-sensitive and -insensitive ER<sup>+</sup> BrCa xenografts

The effects of combining palbociclib with a CDK8/19i on tumor growth <italic>in vivo</italic> were investigated using the MCF-7 xenograft model, which was treated for up to 80 days with vehicle control, 50 mg/kg/d palbociclib, 30 mg/kg/d SNX631-6, or a combination of the two drugs. <sentence_start/>Palbociclib significantly inhibited tumor growth, but after ∼60 days of treatment, the slope of the tumor growth curve increased by up to 5-fold in the palbociclib arm (Figure 3A), indicating the development of adaptive drug resistance. <sentence_start/>SNX631-6 alone had only a moderate, albeit significant, effect on tumor growth (Figure 3A). <sentence_start/>Nevertheless, morphological analysis of the tumors collected at the endpoint indicated that 8/10 control MCF-7 tumors were highly invasive, showing tumor penetration of the muscle layer, whereas muscle invasion was detected in only 2/10 tumors treated with SNX631-6 alone (Figures 3B and S5A). <sentence_start/>These results, in concordance with similar observations on the effect of a CDK8/19i on invasive growth in a transgenic breast cancer model,<citation rid="bib46" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41388-018-0316-y" pmid="29780169" pmcid="PMC7018387" count="1"><sup>46</sup></citation> indicate that CDK8/19 inhibition suppresses tumor invasion, even when it has only a modest effect Hence, prevention of adaptive palbociclib resistance by CDK8/19 inhibition appears to involve both the suppression of transcriptional reprogramming associated with the development of resistance and downregulation of several tumor-supporting genes by the combination of CDK4/6i and CDK8/19i.
Discussion

In the present study, we found that the adaptive resistance to different CDK4/6i rapidly develops <italic>in vitro</italic> and <italic>in vivo</italic>, with similar rapid kinetics in different ER<sup>+</sup> BrCa and other tumor cell lines. <sentence_start/>Luria-Delbrück fluctuation analysis showed fluctuating short-term palbociclib sensitivity among 44 MCF-7 clones, with no resistant outliers indicative of a heritable pre-resistant phenotype. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, both mass populations and individual clones lost resistance after drug withdrawal, supporting a transient, non-genetic mechanism. <sentence_start/>Ten independently adapted MCF-7 populations exhibited remarkably similar transcriptomic changes. <sentence_start/>This similarity most likely reflects concordant transcriptional reprogramming, rather than a selection of stable pre-existing variants, because scRNA-seq data from 977 untreated MCF-7 cells revealed no drug-naive cells with transcriptomic markers of palbociclib adaptation.

Adaptive palbociclib resistance <italic>in vitro</italic> was associated with a pseudo-senescent phenotype. <sentence_start/>Despite displaying senescence markers, adapted cells continued to divide, although with delayed G1 progression and fewer mitoses, potentially reflecting downregulation of the MYC pathway. <sentence_start/>Frequent replating, which preferentially removes highly adherent cells with senescent morphology, prevented adaptation during prolonged palbociclib treatment. <sentence_start/>This finding suggests that senescent-like cells contribute to adaptation, possibly through paracrine SASP effects.<citation rid="bib22" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41580-024-00727-x" pmid="38654098" count="1"><sup>22</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Remarkably, interferon signaling is known to be a major trigger of SASP,<citation rid="bib58" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1096/fj.202400808RR" pmid="39157951" count="1"><sup>58</sup></citation> and interferon pathways were drastically upregulated in cells that were adapted to palbociclib <italic>in vitro</italic> and <italic>in vivo</italic>. <sentence_start/>Specifically, IFN-γ, IFN-α, and TNF-α signaling via NF-κB were the top three most upregulated pathways by palbociclib <italic>in vivo</italic>. <sentence_start/>A possible cause of the upregulation of these pathways could be the activation of retrotransposons carrying repeat sequences that activate cGAS-STING, leading to interferon pathway activation and the acquisition of drug resistance.<citation rid="bib49" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.2213146119" pmcid="PMC9894111" pmid="36449545" count="1"><sup>50</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Our RNA-seq analysis was carried out on poly(A)<sup>+</sup> RNA and, therefore, could not be used to analyze the repeatome components, but we found that the cGAS-STING pathway was activated in P-A xenografts, in accordance with the retrotransposon activation hypothesis.

Given the known role of transcriptional changes in the resistance to CDK4/6i, we tested if such resistance would be prevented by the inhibition of CDK8/19 Mediator kinases, pleiotropic regulators of transcriptional reprogramming. <sentence_start/>In contrast to pleiotropic transcriptional inhibitors, such as inhibitors of CDK7 and CDK9, CDK8/19i alone had only limited and variable antiproliferative effects, and their combination with CDK4/6i showed no reproducible evidence of synergistic or even additive effects in shorter-term (7-day) studies. <sentence_start/>However, CDK8/19i prevented the development of CDK4/6i resistance in prolonged assays, a highly specific effect of CDK8/19 inhibition. <sentence_start/>The prevention of resistance was observed in different cell lines, both in drug-naive and in P-A cells, and in all MCF-7 clones with different levels of palbociclib sensitivity. <sentence_start/>The antiproliferative effects of CDK4/6i and CDK8/19i combination, like the effects of CDK4/6i alone, remained dependent on Rb, as demonstrated by the more rapid loss of Rb in cells treated with the drug combination and by reduced sensitivity to this combination in cells with Rb knockdown.

Treatment with the CDK8/19i also potentiated the effects of CDK4/6i <italic>in vivo</italic>, with the effects of the addition of CDK8/19i SNX631-6 consistent with the prevention of palbociclib resistance in MCF-7 xenografts, where the effect of CDK4/6i alone was initially strong, whereas the CDK8/19i alone had only a modest effect. <sentence_start/>Remarkably, long-term synergy between palbociclib and SNX631-6 was observed even in xenografts formed by T-47D cells, which were insensitive to either drug <italic>in vitro</italic>, although both of the individual drugs, especially SNX631-6, had a significant effect on these cells <italic>in vivo</italic>, in agreement with the preferential <italic>in vivo</italic> sensitivity to CDK8/19i observed in triple-negative breast cancer.<citation rid="bib34" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.2414501121" pmcid="PMC11588072" pmid="39541354" count="1"><sup>34</sup></citation>

Most of the transcriptomic changes in cells adapted to palbociclib <italic>in vitro</italic> arose late, limiting the analysis of the effects of the drug’s combination with CDK8/19i, as the combination-treated cells did not survive long enough for analysis. <sentence_start/>However, we were able to analyze the transcriptomic effects of the drug combination on the development of long-term palbociclib resistance <italic>in vivo</italic>. <sentence_start/>The addition of the CDK8/19i to palbociclib had two major effects at the level of pathways and individual genes. <sentence_start/>The first effect was reduced upregulation of the genes and pathways associated with tumor growth in the presence of palbociclib. <sentence_start/>This was observed for several pathways that regulate gene expression, such as TGF-β signaling, hedgehog signaling, Notch signaling, and Wnt/β-catenin signaling, as well as the cGAS-STING pathway, a probable upstream inducer of the interferon pathways. <sentence_start/>Remarkably, the addition of a CDK8/19i decreased the upregulation of all 12 pathways that were upregulated both in palbociclib-treated MCF-7 xenografts and the ZR75-1 xenografts treated with a selective CDK4 inhibitor, atirmociclib.<citation rid="bib5" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ccell.2025.02.006" pmid="40068598" count="1"><sup>5</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Several of these pathways, including TNF-α-NF-κB signaling, IL-6-JAK-STAT3 signaling, inflammatory response, angiogenesis, epithelial-mesenchymal transition, and estrogen response, have been previously reported to be positively regulated by CDK8/19.<citation rid="bib25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.1710467114" pmid="28855340" pmcid="PMC5617299" count="1"><sup>25</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.18632/oncotarget.14894" pmid="28147342" pmcid="PMC5355036" count="1"><sup>26</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib46" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41388-018-0316-y" pmid="29780169" pmcid="PMC7018387" count="1"><sup>46</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib59" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.immuni.2012.10.017" pmid="23352233" pmcid="PMC3580287" count="1"><sup>59</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib60" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/gtc.12475" pmid="28151579" count="1"><sup>60</sup></citation><sup>,</sup><citation rid="bib61" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.yexcr.2018.05.033" pmid="29856990" count="1"><sup>61</sup></citation> At the individual-gene level, CDK8/19i suppressed palbociclib-induced CDK6 expression both <italic>in vitro</italic> and <italic>in vivo</italic>, as well as the induction of several other tumor-promoting or CDK4/6i resistance-associated genes, including <italic>SLC12A7</italic>, <italic>RAB11FIP4</italic>, <italic>OXTR</italic>, <italic>EGR1</italic>, and <italic>VWA7</italic>, indicating that the inhibition of CDK8/19-mediated transcriptional reprogramming affects multiple markers and mechanisms of resistance to CDK4/6-targeting drugs. <sentence_start/>The second major effect was specific to the drug combination and included induction of keratin genes and the oxidative phosphorylation pathway, together with suppression of the mitotic-spindle and G2/M-checkpoint pathways associated with cell proliferation. <sentence_start/>Remarkably, individual genes that were most strongly and selectively downregulated by the drug combination, such as <italic>UGDH</italic>, <italic>IRS1</italic>, and <italic>INSR</italic>, have known tumor-promoting activities. <sentence_start/>Hence, CDK8/19i offer long-term potentiation of CDK4/6-targeting drugs both by interfering with transcriptional reprogramming associated with tumor cell adaptation to the latter drugs and by the specific effects of the CDK4/6 and CDK8/19i combination on genes that regulate tumor growth.

These findings support the therapeutic potential of combining inhibitors of CDK4/6 and CDK8/19. <sentence_start/>CDK4/6i are used for the treatment of ER<sup>+</sup> BrCa in combination with antiestrogens, and the addition of CDK8/19i to this combination is likely to be especially beneficial, given the known co-operative effect of CDK8/19i and antiestrogens.<citation rid="bib26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.18632/oncotarget.14894" pmid="28147342" pmcid="PMC5355036" count="1"><sup>26</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>CDK4/6i are also being actively investigated for the treatment of other malignancies, where their combination with CDK8/19i is also likely to be beneficial.
Limitations of the study

Our study has several limitations. <sentence_start/>First, although we observed consistent effects across multiple established breast cancer cell line models, these systems do not fully recapitulate the heterogeneity of human tumors. <sentence_start/>Future studies using patient-derived xenografts and organoid models are important to further evaluate the translational potential of CDK8/19 inhibitors in combination with CDK4/6 inhibitors. <sentence_start/>Second, while our studies revealed the ability of CDK8/19 inhibitor to suppress transcriptional reprogramming associated with the adaptation to palbociclib <italic>in vivo</italic>, we were unable to perform long-term transcriptomic analyses of the CDK4/6-CDK8/19 inhibitor combination <italic>in vitro</italic> because the strong efficacy of the combination largely prevented the emergence of adapted cell populations. <sentence_start/>In addition, our <italic>in vivo</italic> efficacy studies were performed in NSG mice and, therefore, did not permit assessment of tumor-immune interactions. <sentence_start/>Future studies in immunocompetent models are needed to determine how CDK8/19 inhibition affects CDK4/6 inhibitor-induced remodeling of the breast tumor microenvironment, antitumor immunity, and therapeutic response. <sentence_start/>Finally, because our RNA-seq analysis was restricted to poly(A)<sup>+</sup> transcripts, we were unable to comprehensively analyze the repeatome or directly assess retrotransposon activation. <sentence_start/>Future studies employing total RNA-seq, long-read sequencing, or dedicated repeatome analyses are necessary to determine whether activation of transposable elements contributes to the interferon and cGAS-STING signatures observed during adaptation.

Cell proliferation assays

Cells were seeded into 96-well plates (1,500 cells/well). <sentence_start/>After 24 h, cells were treated with palbociclib (4 nM-1 μM or 16 nM-4 μM), alone or in combination with SNX631 (500 nM). <sentence_start/>After 7 days, cell densities were measured by sulforhodamine B sodium salt (SRB) assay. <sentence_start/>For 20-day SRB time course assays, culture media were replaced every 5 days. <sentence_start/>For flask assays, cells were seeded into T25 flasks (250,000 cells/flask for the lower-dose SNX631 study; 600,000 cells/flask for the higher-dose Senexin B study). <sentence_start/>Vehicle control- and 500 nM SNX631-treated flasks were stained with crystal violet when the vehicle control flask reached 100% confluence. <sentence_start/>500 nM palbociclib- and 500 nM palbociclib+SNX631-treated flasks were stained with crystal violet when the combination flask was estimated to contain no viable cells. <sentence_start/>Crystal violet images are representative of three separate biological replicates. <sentence_start/>For 20-day raw cell counting experiments, cells were seeded into duplicate flasks per condition (125,000 cells per flask) and treated with the appropriate drug conditions the day after seeding. <sentence_start/>Culture media were replaced every 7 days with fresh, drug-containing media. <sentence_start/>At each indicated time point, duplicate flasks were trypsinized, and total live cell numbers were counted by Bio-Rad TC10 automated cell counter with trypan blue dye. <sentence_start/>For 25-day endpoint analysis, triplicate flasks per condition were trypsinized and counted, and a fourth replicate flask was stained with crystal violet.
Bliss synergy analysis

Bliss synergy analysis was performed to assess the interaction between Palbociclib and SNX631 in MCF-7 cells. <sentence_start/>Cells were treated with each drug alone and in combination at the indicated concentrations, and cell viability was measured following the specified treatment period and normalized to untreated controls. <sentence_start/>The expected combined effect under the Bliss independence model (E_bliss) was calculated as E_bliss = E_A + E_B − (E_A × E_B), where E_A and E_B represent the fractional effects of Palbociclib and SNX631, respectively. <sentence_start/>Bliss scores were determined by comparing the observed combination effect to the expected effect, with positive values indicating synergy, negative values indicating antagonism, and values near zero indicating additive effects.
